CVE-2026-60010.title: Repo-side team-link endpoint still bypasses RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess
CVE-2026-60010.description: ### Summary `PUT /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/teams/{team}` allows a non-owner repository admin to attach organization teams to a repository even when the organization has disabled that behaviour with `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess=false`. An earlier advisory fixed the corresponding team-side endpoint; the repository-side endpoint retained the weaker check. ### Details The repository-side handler's exception relies on a repository permission check (`IsOwner()`), which for an organization repository is satisfied by a user promoted to owner-level access through an attached admin team. The fixed team-side endpoint instead checks actual organization ownership when `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess` is disabled. The matching web collaboration-settings handler had the same weak check. ### Impact A user with delegated admin rights on one organization repository can grant other organization teams read or write access to that repository without approval from an actual organization owner, exposing private source and history and, for a write-capable team, granting push access. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39046, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66849.title: Package registry: restricted users can read packages of limited-visibility users (authorization bypass)
CVE-2026-66849.description: ### Summary The package-registry access check grants read access to a package owned by a Limited-visibility user to any non-ghost logged-in user, without excluding restricted accounts. A restricted account can therefore enumerate and download the entire package registry (for example Docker, npm, PyPI) of any Limited-visibility user. ### Details The user-owner branch of `determineAccessMode` omits the restricted-user check that the organization-owner branch and the repository permission model apply. ### Impact Authorization boundary / confidentiality. A restricted account can read package content of Limited-visibility users that it should not be able to see. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39043, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66853.title: Restricted users can enumerate limited-visibility organizations via the user org-list API (authorization bypass)
CVE-2026-66853.description: ### Summary A restricted account can enumerate Limited-visibility organizations and their name, description and avatar by listing the public organization memberships of a known user through `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/orgs`. ### Details The helper that decides which organization visibilities to include for the viewer returns 'Limited' for any signed-in, non-admin, non-self viewer without excluding restricted accounts, so the response admits both public and limited organizations. The single-organization endpoint `GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}` correctly returns `404` to a restricted viewer for a limited organization; the list path uses a different, unrestricted helper. ### Impact Authorization boundary / confidentiality. A restricted account, which by policy may reach only public content, can discover Limited-visibility organizations and their metadata by walking the public memberships of known users. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39047, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66874.title: A fork pull request author can satisfy a required Actions status check without any workflow running, because a filtered out workflow taken from the pull request HEAD posts a `skipped` commit status that counts as success
CVE-2026-66874.description: ### Summary Gitea writes a synthetic `skipped` commit status for a workflow that matched an event but was excluded by its own `branches:` or `paths:` filter, so that a required status check tied to that workflow does not block indefinitely. For a `pull_request` event the workflow definition is read from the pull request head commit, which for a fork pull request is controlled by the pull request author. The author can define a workflow whose name matches a required status check context and give it a filter that never matches, causing Gitea to write a `skipped` status under that context on the base repository. Because `skipped` counts as success when statuses are combined, the required check evaluates as passed. ### Details This path deliberately creates no workflow run, so the fork approval gate, which guards run creation, does not apply. No write access, runner or approval is required. The required context string is publicly visible as the check name on any pull request. ### Impact Bypass of branch-protection required status checks and of organization-mandated required workflows. Code can reach a protected branch with mandated checks shown as passing although nothing ran; where auto-merge is scheduled it can merge unattended. Any authenticated user who can fork and open a pull request is a potential actor. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds None that preserve the protection. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66877.title: RCE on self-hosted runners | fork-PR approval gate (`NeedApproval`) bypass via job-level concurrency cancellation
CVE-2026-66877.description: ### Summary Workflow runs from first-time fork contributors are held for maintainer approval only by inserting the run's jobs in a blocked state. The component that transitions blocked jobs to waiting does not re-check whether the run still needs approval. A separate, legitimate run in the same repository that shares a job-level `concurrency` group with the pending run can cause the pending run to be re-evaluated, which unblocks and dispatches its remaining jobs to runners without approval. Any user who can open a pull request can reach this. ### Details The approval decision itself is correct, but it is enforced purely as job status. The job emitter, the concurrency-preparation path and the runner task-pickup path do not check approval; only the concurrency-wake path did. Cancelling one job of the pending run through the shared job-level concurrency group triggers a re-emit over that run's still-blocked sibling jobs, which are then moved to waiting and picked up by runners. ### Impact Arbitrary, unreviewed workflow code execution on the self-hosted runners of any repository that accepts fork pull requests, defeating the first-time-contributor approval boundary. Fork pull request secrets remain withheld and the run token remains read-only; the impact is access to the runner host (internal network reachability, runner-local caches, workspaces and credentials, and persistence into later trusted builds). ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds Instances that do not run fork pull request workflows on self-hosted runners are not exposed to the code-execution impact. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73130.title: Unbounded gitignores repository-creation field enables linear template-read amplification
CVE-2026-73130.description: ### Summary The `gitignores` field of the repository-creation form and API option struct has no maximum-length constraint. During repository initialization the field is split on commas and each name triggers a template read whose result is buffered in memory before `.gitignore` is written. A large attacker-controlled value therefore produces a proportional number of template reads and in-memory buffering. ### Details Reachable through `POST /repo/create` and `POST /api/v1/user/repos` (and the organization equivalent) when auto-init is enabled. ### Impact Uncontrolled resource consumption during repository creation, proportional to the submitted field length. Availability only. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39027, #39040). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73135.title: Repository listing exposes repositories owned by hidden users due to inconsistent visibility predicate
CVE-2026-73135.description: ### Summary Gitea implements repository visibility with several SQL predicates that are meant to be equivalent. One of them, used by the accessible-repository condition, treats repositories owned by hidden users differently from the others. As a result, some repository-listing endpoints return repositories owned by hidden users even though those repositories are unreachable through their direct routes, which still return `404`. ### Details The authenticated repository-search API is the broadest affected surface; the forks listing is also affected for anonymous users, and watched repositories for users already subscribed. ### Impact Any authenticated user can enumerate repositories owned by hidden users through repository search; anonymous users can do so through the forks listing. Metadata disclosure only. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39009, #39012). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73504.title: Unauthenticated artifact-to-repository oracle in raw Actions downloads
CVE-2026-73504.description: ### Summary The raw Actions artifact download endpoint looks up the artifact row before validating the signed URL. Without authentication, an invalid signature produces one response when the supplied global artifact ID belongs to the named repository (and is upload-confirmed or expired) and a different response when it does not. Because artifact IDs are global auto-incrementing integers, this lets an unauthenticated caller test whether a guessed artifact ID belongs to an already-named private repository. ### Details The signature check still protects artifact bytes; only the ordering of the row lookup and the signature check creates the distinguishable responses. The endpoint does not reveal whether the repository exists, since inaccessible and nonexistent repositories return the same status. ### Impact Unauthenticated confirmation of the association between an artifact ID and a known private repository. Artifact contents are not exposed. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39049, #39053). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73535.title: 2FA bypass and persistent account takeover via OpenID identity linking
CVE-2026-73535.description: The `POST /user/openid/connect` handler did not enforce second-factor authentication. An attacker who knew a victim's password could obtain a full authenticated session by submitting that password through the OpenID connect flow instead of the normal login form, bypassing TOTP and WebAuthn checks entirely. The same request could attach an attacker-controlled OpenID identifier to the victim's account before sign-in completed. Because the OpenID sign-in path also lacked a second-factor check, the attacker could subsequently authenticate using that identifier alone — without the victim's password or second factor. Changing the victim's password did not remove the linked identifier. OpenID sign-in is enabled by default on instances set up through the installer. ## Affected Versions Confirmed on **1.27.1**. All versions that expose the OpenID connect endpoint and support TOTP or WebAuthn second factors should be assumed affected until verified otherwise. ## Impact **Who was affected:** Users on instances with OpenID sign-in enabled who had enrolled TOTP or WebAuthn as a second factor. **What broke:** Second-factor enrollment is intended to make a leaked password survivable. The OpenID connect path removed that protection for enrolled users. Password-based login continued to enforce the second-factor challenge as expected. **Persistent access:** The connect handler wrote the attacker's OpenID identifier to the victim's account before granting the session. Subsequent OpenID sign-ins using that identifier required neither the victim's password nor a second factor. Password rotation did not revoke this access; the linked identifier had to be removed manually from account settings. **`TWO_FACTOR_AUTH = enforced` did not mitigate this.** The enforced setting relied on a session flag set at sign-in time. Because enrolled users were flagged as having completed second-factor setup, hijacked sessions passed the enforced check rather than being challenged again. | Attack vector | Prerequisites | Consequence | |---------------|---------------|-------------| | OpenID connect with password | Victim's password; OpenID sign-in enabled | Full session without second-factor challenge | | OpenID sign-in via linked identifier | Prior successful connect attack | Full session without password or second factor; survives password change | On a compromised Gitea account, an attacker gained access to repositories, CI secrets, Actions configuration, and push permissions for everything the user could write to. Administrator accounts exposed the entire instance. ## Root Cause `ConnectOpenIDPost` (`routers/web/auth/openid.go`) authenticated the user with `auth.UserSignIn`, discarded the returned authentication source (which carries the second-factor policy), linked a new OpenID identifier to the account, and called `handleSignIn` — none of which consulted TOTP or WebAuthn enrollment. The password login handler (`SignInPost` in `routers/web/auth/auth.go`) checked `TwoFactorShouldSkip()`, TOTP enrollment, and WebAuthn registration before granting a session. Those checks were absent from the OpenID connect flow. OpenID 2.0 identities are stored in the `user_openid` table rather than as a configurable authentication source, so there was no per-source setting that could explain the missing enforcement.

CVE-2026-73802.title: gitea-runner: workflow container.options passes host namespaces and capability flags to job container when privileged mode is disabled
CVE-2026-73802.description: ### Summary act_runner appends workflow-controlled `jobs.<job>.container.options` directly to the Docker HostConfig for the job container. When runner privileged mode is disabled, only `Privileged` is forced false. Host namespace flags, capability expansion, and security profile overrides from workflow YAML are preserved in the final HostConfig. A workflow author can enter host PID/IPC namespaces and execute commands on the runner host as root. ### Details Source-to-sink path in act_runner: - `ContainerSpec.Options` accepts workflow YAML `container.options` - `RunContext.options()` appends workflow options to runner-level container options - Job container is created with `Privileged: rc.Config.Privileged` but also with `Options: rc.options(ctx)` - `mergeContainerConfigs()` parses Docker CLI-style options into HostConfig - When privileged mode is disabled, only `copts.privileged` is forced false - `sanitizeConfig()` only filters `Binds` and `Mounts` - Preserved dangerous HostConfig fields: ```text Privileged=false PidMode=host IpcMode=host CapAdd=['ALL'] SecurityOpt=['seccomp=unconfined','apparmor=unconfined'] ``` Attacker workflow YAML: ```yaml jobs: breakout: runs-on: ubuntu-latest container: image: ubuntu:22.04 options: >- --pid=host --ipc=host --cap-add=ALL --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined steps: - name: host namespace marker run: | nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n -p -- sh -c 'id > /tmp/marker' ``` ### Impact An attacker who can submit a workflow to a repository using a shared Docker-backed act_runner can: - Enter host PID, IPC, and mount namespaces - Execute arbitrary commands as root on the runner host - Access runner host secrets, deployment credentials, and environment variables - Pivot to adjacent jobs running on the same runner - Access internal build infrastructure reachable from the runner host Critical severity for shared runners where untrusted users can trigger workflows. High severity for single-tenant runners with privileged mode explicitly disabled as a security control. ### Fix Direction Treat `container.options` as untrusted input. Reject or strip when privileged mode is disabled: - Host namespaces: `--pid=host`, `--ipc=host`, `--uts=host`, `--network=host` - Capability expansion: `--cap-add ALL`, `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` - Security overrides: `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`, `--security-opt apparmor=unconfined` - Device access: `--device`, `--device-cgroup-rule` - Volume inheritance: `--volumes-from` - Runtime controls: `--runtime`, `--cgroup-parent`

CVE-2026-73804.title: User-scoped tokens can mint unscoped HTTP signature API credentials
CVE-2026-73804.description: ### Summary Gitea allow a `write:user` token to create an SSH public key that then authenticates to the API through HTTP Signature without any API token scope. The vulnerable chain is: 1. A token with only `write:user` cannot directly call unrelated API categories such as `write:admin`. 2. The same token can call `POST /api/v1/user/keys` and add an attacker-controlled SSH public key to the token owner's account. 3. The matching private key can sign API requests through Gitea's HTTP Signature authentication. 4. `HTTPSign.Verify()` authenticates the request as the key owner and sets `IsApiToken=true`, but it does not set `ApiTokenScope`. 5. `tokenRequiresScopes()` skips route-level scope enforcement when `IsApiToken=true` but `ApiTokenScope` is absent. The result is a token-to-credential escalation. The attacker starts with a user-scoped token and ends with an unscoped API authentication method for the same account. The resulting access is still constrained by the account's normal Gitea RBAC, but it bypasses the API token scope boundary. ### Details The API auth group accepts HTTP Signature authentication for API routes: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:769-780 func buildAuthGroup() *auth.Group { group := auth.NewGroup( &auth.OAuth2{}, &auth.HTTPSign{}, &auth.Basic{}, // FIXME: this should be removed once we don't allow basic auth in API ) if setting.Service.EnableReverseProxyAuthAPI { group.Add(&auth.ReverseProxy{}) // TODO: does it still make sense to support reverse proxy auth in API? } // others: API doesn't support SSPI auth because the caller should use token return group } ``` When a request contains a valid HTTP Signature, Gitea resolves the SSH key owner and marks the request as API-token authenticated: ```go // services/auth/httpsign.go:39-86 // Verify extracts and validates HTTPsign from the Signature header of the request and returns // the corresponding user object on successful validation. // Returns nil if header is empty or validation fails. func (h *HTTPSign) Verify(req *http.Request, w http.ResponseWriter, store DataStore, sess SessionStore) (*user_model.User, error) { sigHead := req.Header.Get('Signature') if len(sigHead) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } var ( publicKey *asymkey_model.PublicKey err error ) if len(req.Header.Get('X-Ssh-Certificate')) != 0 { // Handle Signature signed by SSH certificates if len(setting.SSH.TrustedUserCAKeys) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } publicKey, err = VerifyCert(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyCert on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } else { // Handle Signature signed by Public Key publicKey, err = VerifyPubKey(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyPubKey on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } u, err := user_model.GetUserByID(req.Context(), publicKey.OwnerID) if err != nil { log.Error('GetUserByID: %v', err) return nil, err } store.GetData()['IsApiToken'] = true log.Trace('HTTP Sign: Logged in user %-v', u) return u, nil } ``` That path does not assign `ApiTokenScope`. The route-level scope middleware is fail-open for that state. It only checks required scopes when both `IsApiToken=true` and `ApiTokenScope` exists: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:319-363 func tokenRequiresScopes(requiredScopeCategories ...auth_model.AccessTokenScopeCategory) func(ctx *context.APIContext) { return func(ctx *context.APIContext) { // no scope required if len(requiredScopeCategories) == 0 { return } // Need OAuth2 token to be present. scope, scopeExists := ctx.Data['ApiTokenScope'].(auth_model.AccessTokenScope) if ctx.Data['IsApiToken'] != true || !scopeExists { return } // use the http method to determine the access level requiredScopeLevel := auth_model.Read if ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPost || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPut || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPatch || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodDelete { requiredScopeLevel = auth_model.Write } // get the required scope for the given access level and category requiredScopes := auth_model.GetRequiredScopes(requiredScopeLevel, requiredScopeCategories...) allow, err := scope.HasScope(requiredScopes...) if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'checking scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } if !allow { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, fmt.Sprintf('token does not have at least one of required scope(s), required=%v, token scope=%v', requiredScopes, scope)) return } ctx.Data['requiredScopeCategories'] = requiredScopeCategories // check if scope only applies to public resources publicOnly, err := scope.PublicOnly() if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'parsing public resource scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } // assign to true so that those searching should only filter public repositories/users/organizations ctx.PublicOnly = publicOnly } } ``` Therefore, a signed HTTP Signature request proceeds to the handler and normal account RBAC without checking `write:admin`, `write:repository`, `write:organization`, or other token categories. The key-enrollment route is available through the user scope group: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:1086-1091 m.Group('/keys', func() { m.Combo('').Get(user.ListMyPublicKeys). Post(bind(api.CreateKeyOption{}), user.CreatePublicKey) m.Combo('/{id}').Get(user.GetPublicKey). Delete(user.DeletePublicKey) }, rejectPublicOnly()) ``` `CreatePublicKey()` stores the supplied key for the authenticated user: ```go // routers/api/v1/user/key.go:202-249 func CreateUserPublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext, form api.CreateKeyOption, uid int64) { if user_model.IsFeatureDisabledWithLoginType(ctx.Doer, setting.UserFeatureManageSSHKeys) { ctx.APIErrorNotFound('Not Found', errors.New('ssh keys setting is not allowed to be visited')) return } content, err := asymkey_model.CheckPublicKeyString(form.Key) if err != nil { repo.HandleCheckKeyStringError(ctx, err) return } key, err := asymkey_model.AddPublicKey(ctx, uid, form.Title, content, 0, false) if err != nil { repo.HandleAddKeyError(ctx, err) return } apiLink := composePublicKeysAPILink() apiKey := convert.ToPublicKey(apiLink, key) if ctx.Doer.IsAdmin || ctx.Doer.ID == key.OwnerID { apiKey, _ = appendPrivateInformation(ctx, apiKey, key, ctx.Doer) } ctx.JSON(http.StatusCreated, apiKey) } // CreatePublicKey create one public key for me func CreatePublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext) { // swagger:operation POST /user/keys user userCurrentPostKey // --- // summary: Create a public key // consumes: // - application/json // produces: // - application/json // parameters: // - name: body // in: body // schema: // '$ref': '#/definitions/CreateKeyOption' // responses: // '201': // '$ref': '#/responses/PublicKey' // '422': // '$ref': '#/responses/validationError' form := web.GetForm(ctx).(*api.CreateKeyOption) CreateUserPublicKey(ctx, *form, ctx.Doer.ID) } ``` This means a `write:user` token can enroll an attacker-controlled key, and that key then becomes an unscoped HTTP Signature API credential. ### PoC ```http # Control: the original write:user token cannot directly use admin scope. POST /api/v1/admin/users Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'username':'scope-control','email':'scope-control@example.invalid','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'scope-control','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 403 Forbidden # Enroll an attacker-controlled SSH public key with the same write:user token. POST /api/v1/user/keys Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'title':'httpsig-api-key','key':'ssh-rsa {attacker-public-key}'} # Expected: 201 Created # Sign an admin API request with the matching private key. The Signature keyId is # the SSH fingerprint of the enrolled public key, and the signed headers include # (request-target), (created), and (expires). POST /api/v1/admin/users Signature: keyId='{ssh-key-fingerprint}',algorithm='{ssh-signature-algorithm}',headers='(request-target) (created) (expires)',signature='{base64-signature}' Content-Type: application/json {'username':'created-by-httpsig','email':'created-by-httpsig@example.com','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'created-by-httpsig','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 201 Created when the key owner is a site admin ``` ### Impact The attacker can enroll an SSH key and use HTTP Signature to reach any API category allowed by the victim account's normal RBAC. For a site-admin victim, the PoC shows access to `POST /api/v1/admin/users` without `write:admin`. For a non-admin victim, the same unscoped HTTP Signature credential can reach repository, package, organization, issue, or notification APIs according to the user's account permissions, without the corresponding token scopes. Destructive operations are also available where the victim account has the corresponding RBAC, such as repository/package deletion or admin-managed resource changes.

CVE-2026-59774.title: Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Read can lead to RCE
CVE-2026-59774.description: ### Summary An unauthenticated remote attacker can submit Org-mode markup containing a #+INCLUDE directive to POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup for any suitable public repository to read arbitrary server files. By extracting INTERNAL_TOKEN from app.ini, they can inject a Git hook through the internal logger and achieve command execution as the Gitea OS user during an anonymous clone. ### Details Gitea registers `POST /{username}/{reponame}/markup` with optional sign-in, repository assignment, and a repository-unit reader check. An anonymous user passes that check for a public repository with a normal readable code unit. The handler passes the supplied `Mode`, `Text`, and `FilePath` into Gitea's generic markup renderer. Selecting `Mode: file` and a `.org` filename chooses the Org-mode renderer. Gitea 1.27.0 initializes `go-org` using `org.New()` and does not replace its default `ReadFile` callback. In `go-org` 1.9.1, that callback is `ioutil.ReadFile`; `#+INCLUDE` accepts absolute paths and passes them directly to that callback. #### Preconditions - At least one repository is publicly readable and exposes a unit accepted by the repository markup route. A normal public repository with its code unit enabled satisfies this condition. - Standard Gitea storage permissions allow the service user to update Gitea's managed global Git configuration. ### Impact - Read arbitrary files accessible to the Gitea service user without an account. - Submit the file-read payload directly through a public repository's web markup route without committing a file or obtaining repository write access. - Expose Gitea configuration, internal bearer tokens, OAuth/JWT material, and deployment metadata ### Affected - The vulnerable version seem v1.22.1 ~ v1.27.0 ### Credit Found by @xbow-security. Triaged by Guido Leo <guido.leo@xbow.com>. Independently reported by https://github.com/NightRang3r

CVE-2026-60010.title: Repo-side team-link endpoint still bypasses RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess
CVE-2026-60010.description: ### Summary `PUT /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/teams/{team}` allows a non-owner repository admin to attach organization teams to a repository even when the organization has disabled that behaviour with `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess=false`. An earlier advisory fixed the corresponding team-side endpoint; the repository-side endpoint retained the weaker check. ### Details The repository-side handler's exception relies on a repository permission check (`IsOwner()`), which for an organization repository is satisfied by a user promoted to owner-level access through an attached admin team. The fixed team-side endpoint instead checks actual organization ownership when `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess` is disabled. The matching web collaboration-settings handler had the same weak check. ### Impact A user with delegated admin rights on one organization repository can grant other organization teams read or write access to that repository without approval from an actual organization owner, exposing private source and history and, for a write-capable team, granting push access. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39046, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66849.title: Package registry: restricted users can read packages of limited-visibility users (authorization bypass)
CVE-2026-66849.description: ### Summary The package-registry access check grants read access to a package owned by a Limited-visibility user to any non-ghost logged-in user, without excluding restricted accounts. A restricted account can therefore enumerate and download the entire package registry (for example Docker, npm, PyPI) of any Limited-visibility user. ### Details The user-owner branch of `determineAccessMode` omits the restricted-user check that the organization-owner branch and the repository permission model apply. ### Impact Authorization boundary / confidentiality. A restricted account can read package content of Limited-visibility users that it should not be able to see. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39043, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66853.title: Restricted users can enumerate limited-visibility organizations via the user org-list API (authorization bypass)
CVE-2026-66853.description: ### Summary A restricted account can enumerate Limited-visibility organizations and their name, description and avatar by listing the public organization memberships of a known user through `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/orgs`. ### Details The helper that decides which organization visibilities to include for the viewer returns 'Limited' for any signed-in, non-admin, non-self viewer without excluding restricted accounts, so the response admits both public and limited organizations. The single-organization endpoint `GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}` correctly returns `404` to a restricted viewer for a limited organization; the list path uses a different, unrestricted helper. ### Impact Authorization boundary / confidentiality. A restricted account, which by policy may reach only public content, can discover Limited-visibility organizations and their metadata by walking the public memberships of known users. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39047, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66874.title: A fork pull request author can satisfy a required Actions status check without any workflow running, because a filtered out workflow taken from the pull request HEAD posts a `skipped` commit status that counts as success
CVE-2026-66874.description: ### Summary Gitea writes a synthetic `skipped` commit status for a workflow that matched an event but was excluded by its own `branches:` or `paths:` filter, so that a required status check tied to that workflow does not block indefinitely. For a `pull_request` event the workflow definition is read from the pull request head commit, which for a fork pull request is controlled by the pull request author. The author can define a workflow whose name matches a required status check context and give it a filter that never matches, causing Gitea to write a `skipped` status under that context on the base repository. Because `skipped` counts as success when statuses are combined, the required check evaluates as passed. ### Details This path deliberately creates no workflow run, so the fork approval gate, which guards run creation, does not apply. No write access, runner or approval is required. The required context string is publicly visible as the check name on any pull request. ### Impact Bypass of branch-protection required status checks and of organization-mandated required workflows. Code can reach a protected branch with mandated checks shown as passing although nothing ran; where auto-merge is scheduled it can merge unattended. Any authenticated user who can fork and open a pull request is a potential actor. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds None that preserve the protection. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66877.title: RCE on self-hosted runners | fork-PR approval gate (`NeedApproval`) bypass via job-level concurrency cancellation
CVE-2026-66877.description: ### Summary Workflow runs from first-time fork contributors are held for maintainer approval only by inserting the run's jobs in a blocked state. The component that transitions blocked jobs to waiting does not re-check whether the run still needs approval. A separate, legitimate run in the same repository that shares a job-level `concurrency` group with the pending run can cause the pending run to be re-evaluated, which unblocks and dispatches its remaining jobs to runners without approval. Any user who can open a pull request can reach this. ### Details The approval decision itself is correct, but it is enforced purely as job status. The job emitter, the concurrency-preparation path and the runner task-pickup path do not check approval; only the concurrency-wake path did. Cancelling one job of the pending run through the shared job-level concurrency group triggers a re-emit over that run's still-blocked sibling jobs, which are then moved to waiting and picked up by runners. ### Impact Arbitrary, unreviewed workflow code execution on the self-hosted runners of any repository that accepts fork pull requests, defeating the first-time-contributor approval boundary. Fork pull request secrets remain withheld and the run token remains read-only; the impact is access to the runner host (internal network reachability, runner-local caches, workspaces and credentials, and persistence into later trusted builds). ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds Instances that do not run fork pull request workflows on self-hosted runners are not exposed to the code-execution impact. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73130.title: Unbounded gitignores repository-creation field enables linear template-read amplification
CVE-2026-73130.description: ### Summary The `gitignores` field of the repository-creation form and API option struct has no maximum-length constraint. During repository initialization the field is split on commas and each name triggers a template read whose result is buffered in memory before `.gitignore` is written. A large attacker-controlled value therefore produces a proportional number of template reads and in-memory buffering. ### Details Reachable through `POST /repo/create` and `POST /api/v1/user/repos` (and the organization equivalent) when auto-init is enabled. ### Impact Uncontrolled resource consumption during repository creation, proportional to the submitted field length. Availability only. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39027, #39040). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73135.title: Repository listing exposes repositories owned by hidden users due to inconsistent visibility predicate
CVE-2026-73135.description: ### Summary Gitea implements repository visibility with several SQL predicates that are meant to be equivalent. One of them, used by the accessible-repository condition, treats repositories owned by hidden users differently from the others. As a result, some repository-listing endpoints return repositories owned by hidden users even though those repositories are unreachable through their direct routes, which still return `404`. ### Details The authenticated repository-search API is the broadest affected surface; the forks listing is also affected for anonymous users, and watched repositories for users already subscribed. ### Impact Any authenticated user can enumerate repositories owned by hidden users through repository search; anonymous users can do so through the forks listing. Metadata disclosure only. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39009, #39012). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73504.title: Unauthenticated artifact-to-repository oracle in raw Actions downloads
CVE-2026-73504.description: ### Summary The raw Actions artifact download endpoint looks up the artifact row before validating the signed URL. Without authentication, an invalid signature produces one response when the supplied global artifact ID belongs to the named repository (and is upload-confirmed or expired) and a different response when it does not. Because artifact IDs are global auto-incrementing integers, this lets an unauthenticated caller test whether a guessed artifact ID belongs to an already-named private repository. ### Details The signature check still protects artifact bytes; only the ordering of the row lookup and the signature check creates the distinguishable responses. The endpoint does not reveal whether the repository exists, since inaccessible and nonexistent repositories return the same status. ### Impact Unauthenticated confirmation of the association between an artifact ID and a known private repository. Artifact contents are not exposed. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39049, #39053). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73535.title: 2FA bypass and persistent account takeover via OpenID identity linking
CVE-2026-73535.description: The `POST /user/openid/connect` handler did not enforce second-factor authentication. An attacker who knew a victim's password could obtain a full authenticated session by submitting that password through the OpenID connect flow instead of the normal login form, bypassing TOTP and WebAuthn checks entirely. The same request could attach an attacker-controlled OpenID identifier to the victim's account before sign-in completed. Because the OpenID sign-in path also lacked a second-factor check, the attacker could subsequently authenticate using that identifier alone — without the victim's password or second factor. Changing the victim's password did not remove the linked identifier. OpenID sign-in is enabled by default on instances set up through the installer. ## Affected Versions Confirmed on **1.27.1**. All versions that expose the OpenID connect endpoint and support TOTP or WebAuthn second factors should be assumed affected until verified otherwise. ## Impact **Who was affected:** Users on instances with OpenID sign-in enabled who had enrolled TOTP or WebAuthn as a second factor. **What broke:** Second-factor enrollment is intended to make a leaked password survivable. The OpenID connect path removed that protection for enrolled users. Password-based login continued to enforce the second-factor challenge as expected. **Persistent access:** The connect handler wrote the attacker's OpenID identifier to the victim's account before granting the session. Subsequent OpenID sign-ins using that identifier required neither the victim's password nor a second factor. Password rotation did not revoke this access; the linked identifier had to be removed manually from account settings. **`TWO_FACTOR_AUTH = enforced` did not mitigate this.** The enforced setting relied on a session flag set at sign-in time. Because enrolled users were flagged as having completed second-factor setup, hijacked sessions passed the enforced check rather than being challenged again. | Attack vector | Prerequisites | Consequence | |---------------|---------------|-------------| | OpenID connect with password | Victim's password; OpenID sign-in enabled | Full session without second-factor challenge | | OpenID sign-in via linked identifier | Prior successful connect attack | Full session without password or second factor; survives password change | On a compromised Gitea account, an attacker gained access to repositories, CI secrets, Actions configuration, and push permissions for everything the user could write to. Administrator accounts exposed the entire instance. ## Root Cause `ConnectOpenIDPost` (`routers/web/auth/openid.go`) authenticated the user with `auth.UserSignIn`, discarded the returned authentication source (which carries the second-factor policy), linked a new OpenID identifier to the account, and called `handleSignIn` — none of which consulted TOTP or WebAuthn enrollment. The password login handler (`SignInPost` in `routers/web/auth/auth.go`) checked `TwoFactorShouldSkip()`, TOTP enrollment, and WebAuthn registration before granting a session. Those checks were absent from the OpenID connect flow. OpenID 2.0 identities are stored in the `user_openid` table rather than as a configurable authentication source, so there was no per-source setting that could explain the missing enforcement.

CVE-2026-73802.title: gitea-runner: workflow container.options passes host namespaces and capability flags to job container when privileged mode is disabled
CVE-2026-73802.description: ### Summary act_runner appends workflow-controlled `jobs.<job>.container.options` directly to the Docker HostConfig for the job container. When runner privileged mode is disabled, only `Privileged` is forced false. Host namespace flags, capability expansion, and security profile overrides from workflow YAML are preserved in the final HostConfig. A workflow author can enter host PID/IPC namespaces and execute commands on the runner host as root. ### Details Source-to-sink path in act_runner: - `ContainerSpec.Options` accepts workflow YAML `container.options` - `RunContext.options()` appends workflow options to runner-level container options - Job container is created with `Privileged: rc.Config.Privileged` but also with `Options: rc.options(ctx)` - `mergeContainerConfigs()` parses Docker CLI-style options into HostConfig - When privileged mode is disabled, only `copts.privileged` is forced false - `sanitizeConfig()` only filters `Binds` and `Mounts` - Preserved dangerous HostConfig fields: ```text Privileged=false PidMode=host IpcMode=host CapAdd=['ALL'] SecurityOpt=['seccomp=unconfined','apparmor=unconfined'] ``` Attacker workflow YAML: ```yaml jobs: breakout: runs-on: ubuntu-latest container: image: ubuntu:22.04 options: >- --pid=host --ipc=host --cap-add=ALL --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined steps: - name: host namespace marker run: | nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n -p -- sh -c 'id > /tmp/marker' ``` ### Impact An attacker who can submit a workflow to a repository using a shared Docker-backed act_runner can: - Enter host PID, IPC, and mount namespaces - Execute arbitrary commands as root on the runner host - Access runner host secrets, deployment credentials, and environment variables - Pivot to adjacent jobs running on the same runner - Access internal build infrastructure reachable from the runner host Critical severity for shared runners where untrusted users can trigger workflows. High severity for single-tenant runners with privileged mode explicitly disabled as a security control. ### Fix Direction Treat `container.options` as untrusted input. Reject or strip when privileged mode is disabled: - Host namespaces: `--pid=host`, `--ipc=host`, `--uts=host`, `--network=host` - Capability expansion: `--cap-add ALL`, `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` - Security overrides: `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`, `--security-opt apparmor=unconfined` - Device access: `--device`, `--device-cgroup-rule` - Volume inheritance: `--volumes-from` - Runtime controls: `--runtime`, `--cgroup-parent`

CVE-2026-73804.title: User-scoped tokens can mint unscoped HTTP signature API credentials
CVE-2026-73804.description: ### Summary Gitea allow a `write:user` token to create an SSH public key that then authenticates to the API through HTTP Signature without any API token scope. The vulnerable chain is: 1. A token with only `write:user` cannot directly call unrelated API categories such as `write:admin`. 2. The same token can call `POST /api/v1/user/keys` and add an attacker-controlled SSH public key to the token owner's account. 3. The matching private key can sign API requests through Gitea's HTTP Signature authentication. 4. `HTTPSign.Verify()` authenticates the request as the key owner and sets `IsApiToken=true`, but it does not set `ApiTokenScope`. 5. `tokenRequiresScopes()` skips route-level scope enforcement when `IsApiToken=true` but `ApiTokenScope` is absent. The result is a token-to-credential escalation. The attacker starts with a user-scoped token and ends with an unscoped API authentication method for the same account. The resulting access is still constrained by the account's normal Gitea RBAC, but it bypasses the API token scope boundary. ### Details The API auth group accepts HTTP Signature authentication for API routes: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:769-780 func buildAuthGroup() *auth.Group { group := auth.NewGroup( &auth.OAuth2{}, &auth.HTTPSign{}, &auth.Basic{}, // FIXME: this should be removed once we don't allow basic auth in API ) if setting.Service.EnableReverseProxyAuthAPI { group.Add(&auth.ReverseProxy{}) // TODO: does it still make sense to support reverse proxy auth in API? } // others: API doesn't support SSPI auth because the caller should use token return group } ``` When a request contains a valid HTTP Signature, Gitea resolves the SSH key owner and marks the request as API-token authenticated: ```go // services/auth/httpsign.go:39-86 // Verify extracts and validates HTTPsign from the Signature header of the request and returns // the corresponding user object on successful validation. // Returns nil if header is empty or validation fails. func (h *HTTPSign) Verify(req *http.Request, w http.ResponseWriter, store DataStore, sess SessionStore) (*user_model.User, error) { sigHead := req.Header.Get('Signature') if len(sigHead) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } var ( publicKey *asymkey_model.PublicKey err error ) if len(req.Header.Get('X-Ssh-Certificate')) != 0 { // Handle Signature signed by SSH certificates if len(setting.SSH.TrustedUserCAKeys) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } publicKey, err = VerifyCert(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyCert on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } else { // Handle Signature signed by Public Key publicKey, err = VerifyPubKey(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyPubKey on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } u, err := user_model.GetUserByID(req.Context(), publicKey.OwnerID) if err != nil { log.Error('GetUserByID: %v', err) return nil, err } store.GetData()['IsApiToken'] = true log.Trace('HTTP Sign: Logged in user %-v', u) return u, nil } ``` That path does not assign `ApiTokenScope`. The route-level scope middleware is fail-open for that state. It only checks required scopes when both `IsApiToken=true` and `ApiTokenScope` exists: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:319-363 func tokenRequiresScopes(requiredScopeCategories ...auth_model.AccessTokenScopeCategory) func(ctx *context.APIContext) { return func(ctx *context.APIContext) { // no scope required if len(requiredScopeCategories) == 0 { return } // Need OAuth2 token to be present. scope, scopeExists := ctx.Data['ApiTokenScope'].(auth_model.AccessTokenScope) if ctx.Data['IsApiToken'] != true || !scopeExists { return } // use the http method to determine the access level requiredScopeLevel := auth_model.Read if ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPost || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPut || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPatch || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodDelete { requiredScopeLevel = auth_model.Write } // get the required scope for the given access level and category requiredScopes := auth_model.GetRequiredScopes(requiredScopeLevel, requiredScopeCategories...) allow, err := scope.HasScope(requiredScopes...) if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'checking scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } if !allow { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, fmt.Sprintf('token does not have at least one of required scope(s), required=%v, token scope=%v', requiredScopes, scope)) return } ctx.Data['requiredScopeCategories'] = requiredScopeCategories // check if scope only applies to public resources publicOnly, err := scope.PublicOnly() if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'parsing public resource scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } // assign to true so that those searching should only filter public repositories/users/organizations ctx.PublicOnly = publicOnly } } ``` Therefore, a signed HTTP Signature request proceeds to the handler and normal account RBAC without checking `write:admin`, `write:repository`, `write:organization`, or other token categories. The key-enrollment route is available through the user scope group: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:1086-1091 m.Group('/keys', func() { m.Combo('').Get(user.ListMyPublicKeys). Post(bind(api.CreateKeyOption{}), user.CreatePublicKey) m.Combo('/{id}').Get(user.GetPublicKey). Delete(user.DeletePublicKey) }, rejectPublicOnly()) ``` `CreatePublicKey()` stores the supplied key for the authenticated user: ```go // routers/api/v1/user/key.go:202-249 func CreateUserPublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext, form api.CreateKeyOption, uid int64) { if user_model.IsFeatureDisabledWithLoginType(ctx.Doer, setting.UserFeatureManageSSHKeys) { ctx.APIErrorNotFound('Not Found', errors.New('ssh keys setting is not allowed to be visited')) return } content, err := asymkey_model.CheckPublicKeyString(form.Key) if err != nil { repo.HandleCheckKeyStringError(ctx, err) return } key, err := asymkey_model.AddPublicKey(ctx, uid, form.Title, content, 0, false) if err != nil { repo.HandleAddKeyError(ctx, err) return } apiLink := composePublicKeysAPILink() apiKey := convert.ToPublicKey(apiLink, key) if ctx.Doer.IsAdmin || ctx.Doer.ID == key.OwnerID { apiKey, _ = appendPrivateInformation(ctx, apiKey, key, ctx.Doer) } ctx.JSON(http.StatusCreated, apiKey) } // CreatePublicKey create one public key for me func CreatePublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext) { // swagger:operation POST /user/keys user userCurrentPostKey // --- // summary: Create a public key // consumes: // - application/json // produces: // - application/json // parameters: // - name: body // in: body // schema: // '$ref': '#/definitions/CreateKeyOption' // responses: // '201': // '$ref': '#/responses/PublicKey' // '422': // '$ref': '#/responses/validationError' form := web.GetForm(ctx).(*api.CreateKeyOption) CreateUserPublicKey(ctx, *form, ctx.Doer.ID) } ``` This means a `write:user` token can enroll an attacker-controlled key, and that key then becomes an unscoped HTTP Signature API credential. ### PoC ```http # Control: the original write:user token cannot directly use admin scope. POST /api/v1/admin/users Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'username':'scope-control','email':'scope-control@example.invalid','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'scope-control','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 403 Forbidden # Enroll an attacker-controlled SSH public key with the same write:user token. POST /api/v1/user/keys Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'title':'httpsig-api-key','key':'ssh-rsa {attacker-public-key}'} # Expected: 201 Created # Sign an admin API request with the matching private key. The Signature keyId is # the SSH fingerprint of the enrolled public key, and the signed headers include # (request-target), (created), and (expires). POST /api/v1/admin/users Signature: keyId='{ssh-key-fingerprint}',algorithm='{ssh-signature-algorithm}',headers='(request-target) (created) (expires)',signature='{base64-signature}' Content-Type: application/json {'username':'created-by-httpsig','email':'created-by-httpsig@example.com','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'created-by-httpsig','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 201 Created when the key owner is a site admin ``` ### Impact The attacker can enroll an SSH key and use HTTP Signature to reach any API category allowed by the victim account's normal RBAC. For a site-admin victim, the PoC shows access to `POST /api/v1/admin/users` without `write:admin`. For a non-admin victim, the same unscoped HTTP Signature credential can reach repository, package, organization, issue, or notification APIs according to the user's account permissions, without the corresponding token scopes. Destructive operations are also available where the victim account has the corresponding RBAC, such as repository/package deletion or admin-managed resource changes.

CVE-2026-59774.title: Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Read can lead to RCE
CVE-2026-59774.description: ### Summary An unauthenticated remote attacker can submit Org-mode markup containing a #+INCLUDE directive to POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup for any suitable public repository to read arbitrary server files. By extracting INTERNAL_TOKEN from app.ini, they can inject a Git hook through the internal logger and achieve command execution as the Gitea OS user during an anonymous clone. ### Details Gitea registers `POST /{username}/{reponame}/markup` with optional sign-in, repository assignment, and a repository-unit reader check. An anonymous user passes that check for a public repository with a normal readable code unit. The handler passes the supplied `Mode`, `Text`, and `FilePath` into Gitea's generic markup renderer. Selecting `Mode: file` and a `.org` filename chooses the Org-mode renderer. Gitea 1.27.0 initializes `go-org` using `org.New()` and does not replace its default `ReadFile` callback. In `go-org` 1.9.1, that callback is `ioutil.ReadFile`; `#+INCLUDE` accepts absolute paths and passes them directly to that callback. #### Preconditions - At least one repository is publicly readable and exposes a unit accepted by the repository markup route. A normal public repository with its code unit enabled satisfies this condition. - Standard Gitea storage permissions allow the service user to update Gitea's managed global Git configuration. ### Impact - Read arbitrary files accessible to the Gitea service user without an account. - Submit the file-read payload directly through a public repository's web markup route without committing a file or obtaining repository write access. - Expose Gitea configuration, internal bearer tokens, OAuth/JWT material, and deployment metadata ### Affected - The vulnerable version seem v1.22.1 ~ v1.27.0 ### Credit Found by @xbow-security. Triaged by Guido Leo <guido.leo@xbow.com>. Independently reported by https://github.com/NightRang3r

CVE-2026-60010.title: Repo-side team-link endpoint still bypasses RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess
CVE-2026-60010.description: ### Summary `PUT /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/teams/{team}` allows a non-owner repository admin to attach organization teams to a repository even when the organization has disabled that behaviour with `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess=false`. CVE-2026-66853.title: Restricted users can enumerate limited-visibility organizations via the user org-list API (authorization bypass)

CVE-2026-66874.title: A fork pull request author can satisfy a required Actions status check without any workflow running, because a filtered out workflow taken from the pull request HEAD posts a `skipped` commit status that counts as success
CVE-2026-66874.description: ### Summary Gitea writes a synthetic `skipped` commit status for a workflow that matched an event but was excluded by its own `branches:` or `paths:` filter, so that a required status check tied to that workflow does not block indefinitely. For a `pull_request` event the workflow definition is read from the pull request head commit, which for a fork pull request is controlled by the pull request author. The author can define a workflow whose name matches a required status check context and give it a filter that never matches, causing Gitea to write a `skipped` status under that context on the base repository. Because `skipped` counts as success when statuses are combined, the required check evaluates as passed. ### Details This path deliberately creates no workflow run, so the fork approval gate, which guards run creation, does not apply. No write access, runner or approval is required. The required context string is publicly visible as the check name on any pull request. ### Impact Bypass of branch-protection required status checks and of organization-mandated required workflows. Code can reach a protected branch with mandated checks shown as passing although nothing ran; where auto-merge is scheduled it can merge unattended. Any authenticated user who can fork and open a pull request is a potential actor. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds None that preserve the protection. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66877.title: RCE on self-hosted runners | fork-PR approval gate (`NeedApproval`) bypass via job-level concurrency cancellation
CVE-2026-66877.description: ### Summary Workflow runs from first-time fork contributors are held for maintainer approval only by inserting the run's jobs in a blocked state. The component that transitions blocked jobs to waiting does not re-check whether the run still needs approval. A separate, legitimate run in the same repository that shares a job-level `concurrency` group with the pending run can cause the pending run to be re-evaluated, which unblocks and dispatches its remaining jobs to runners without approval. Any user who can open a pull request can reach this. ### Details The approval decision itself is correct, but it is enforced purely as job status. The job emitter, the concurrency-preparation path and the runner task-pickup path do not check approval; only the concurrency-wake path did. Cancelling one job of the pending run through the shared job-level concurrency group triggers a re-emit over that run's still-blocked sibling jobs, which are then moved to waiting and picked up by runners. ### Impact Arbitrary, unreviewed workflow code execution on the self-hosted runners of any repository that accepts fork pull requests, defeating the first-time-contributor approval boundary. Fork pull request secrets remain withheld and the run token remains read-only; the impact is access to the runner host (internal network reachability, runner-local caches, workspaces and credentials, and persistence into later trusted builds). ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds Instances that do not run fork pull request workflows on self-hosted runners are not exposed to the code-execution impact. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73130.title: Unbounded gitignores repository-creation field enables linear template-read amplification
CVE-2026-73130.description: ### Summary The `gitignores` field of the repository-creation form and API option struct has no maximum-length constraint. During repository initialization the field is split on commas and each name triggers a template read whose result is buffered in memory before `.gitignore` is written. A large attacker-controlled value therefore produces a proportional number of template reads and in-memory buffering. ### Details Reachable through `POST /repo/create` and `POST /api/v1/user/repos` (and the organization equivalent) when auto-init is enabled. ### Impact Uncontrolled resource consumption during repository creation, proportional to the submitted field length. Availability only. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39027, #39040). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73135.title: Repository listing exposes repositories owned by hidden users due to inconsistent visibility predicate
CVE-2026-73135.description: ### Summary Gitea implements repository visibility with several SQL predicates that are meant to be equivalent. One of them, used by the accessible-repository condition, treats repositories owned by hidden users differently from the others. As a result, some repository-listing endpoints return repositories owned by hidden users even though those repositories are unreachable through their direct routes, which still return `404`. ### Details The authenticated repository-search API is the broadest affected surface; the forks listing is also affected for anonymous users, and watched repositories for users already subscribed. ### Impact Any authenticated user can enumerate repositories owned by hidden users through repository search; anonymous users can do so through the forks listing. Metadata disclosure only. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39009, #39012). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73504.title: Unauthenticated artifact-to-repository oracle in raw Actions downloads
CVE-2026-73504.description: ### Summary The raw Actions artifact download endpoint looks up the artifact row before validating the signed URL. Without authentication, an invalid signature produces one response when the supplied global artifact ID belongs to the named repository (and is upload-confirmed or expired) and a different response when it does not. Because artifact IDs are global auto-incrementing integers, this lets an unauthenticated caller test whether a guessed artifact ID belongs to an already-named private repository. ### Details The signature check still protects artifact bytes; only the ordering of the row lookup and the signature check creates the distinguishable responses. The endpoint does not reveal whether the repository exists, since inaccessible and nonexistent repositories return the same status. ### Impact Unauthenticated confirmation of the association between an artifact ID and a known private repository. Artifact contents are not exposed. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39049, #39053). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73535.title: 2FA bypass and persistent account takeover via OpenID identity linking
CVE-2026-73535.description: The `POST /user/openid/connect` handler did not enforce second-factor authentication. An attacker who knew a victim's password could obtain a full authenticated session by submitting that password through the OpenID connect flow instead of the normal login form, bypassing TOTP and WebAuthn checks entirely. The same request could attach an attacker-controlled OpenID identifier to the victim's account before sign-in completed. Because the OpenID sign-in path also lacked a second-factor check, the attacker could subsequently authenticate using that identifier alone — without the victim's password or second factor. Changing the victim's password did not remove the linked identifier. OpenID sign-in is enabled by default on instances set up through the installer. ## Affected Versions Confirmed on **1.27.1**. All versions that expose the OpenID connect endpoint and support TOTP or WebAuthn second factors should be assumed affected until verified otherwise. ## Impact **Who was affected:** Users on instances with OpenID sign-in enabled who had enrolled TOTP or WebAuthn as a second factor. **What broke:** Second-factor enrollment is intended to make a leaked password survivable. The OpenID connect path removed that protection for enrolled users. Password-based login continued to enforce the second-factor challenge as expected. **Persistent access:** The connect handler wrote the attacker's OpenID identifier to the victim's account before granting the session. Subsequent OpenID sign-ins using that identifier required neither the victim's password nor a second factor. Password rotation did not revoke this access; the linked identifier had to be removed manually from account settings. **`TWO_FACTOR_AUTH = enforced` did not mitigate this.** The enforced setting relied on a session flag set at sign-in time. Because enrolled users were flagged as having completed second-factor setup, hijacked sessions passed the enforced check rather than being challenged again. | Attack vector | Prerequisites | Consequence | |---------------|---------------|-------------| | OpenID connect with password | Victim's password; OpenID sign-in enabled | Full session without second-factor challenge | | OpenID sign-in via linked identifier | Prior successful connect attack | Full session without password or second factor; survives password change | On a compromised Gitea account, an attacker gained access to repositories, CI secrets, Actions configuration, and push permissions for everything the user could write to. Administrator accounts exposed the entire instance. ## Root Cause `ConnectOpenIDPost` (`routers/web/auth/openid.go`) authenticated the user with `auth.UserSignIn`, discarded the returned authentication source (which carries the second-factor policy), linked a new OpenID identifier to the account, and called `handleSignIn` — none of which consulted TOTP or WebAuthn enrollment. The password login handler (`SignInPost` in `routers/web/auth/auth.go`) checked `TwoFactorShouldSkip()`, TOTP enrollment, and WebAuthn registration before granting a session. Those checks were absent from the OpenID connect flow. OpenID 2.0 identities are stored in the `user_openid` table rather than as a configurable authentication source, so there was no per-source setting that could explain the missing enforcement.

CVE-2026-73802.title: gitea-runner: workflow container.options passes host namespaces and capability flags to job container when privileged mode is disabled
CVE-2026-73802.description: ### Summary act_runner appends workflow-controlled `jobs.<job>.container.options` directly to the Docker HostConfig for the job container. When runner privileged mode is disabled, only `Privileged` is forced false. Host namespace flags, capability expansion, and security profile overrides from workflow YAML are preserved in the final HostConfig. A workflow author can enter host PID/IPC namespaces and execute commands on the runner host as root. ### Details Source-to-sink path in act_runner: - `ContainerSpec.Options` accepts workflow YAML `container.options` - `RunContext.options()` appends workflow options to runner-level container options - Job container is created with `Privileged: rc.Config.Privileged` but also with `Options: rc.options(ctx)` - `mergeContainerConfigs()` parses Docker CLI-style options into HostConfig - When privileged mode is disabled, only `copts.privileged` is forced false - `sanitizeConfig()` only filters `Binds` and `Mounts` - Preserved dangerous HostConfig fields: ```text Privileged=false PidMode=host IpcMode=host CapAdd=['ALL'] SecurityOpt=['seccomp=unconfined','apparmor=unconfined'] ``` Attacker workflow YAML: ```yaml jobs: breakout: runs-on: ubuntu-latest container: image: ubuntu:22.04 options: >- --pid=host --ipc=host --cap-add=ALL --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined steps: - name: host namespace marker run: | nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n -p -- sh -c 'id > /tmp/marker' ``` ### Impact An attacker who can submit a workflow to a repository using a shared Docker-backed act_runner can: - Enter host PID, IPC, and mount namespaces - Execute arbitrary commands as root on the runner host - Access runner host secrets, deployment credentials, and environment variables - Pivot to adjacent jobs running on the same runner - Access internal build infrastructure reachable from the runner host Critical severity for shared runners where untrusted users can trigger workflows. High severity for single-tenant runners with privileged mode explicitly disabled as a security control. ### Fix Direction Treat `container.options` as untrusted input. Reject or strip when privileged mode is disabled: - Host namespaces: `--pid=host`, `--ipc=host`, `--uts=host`, `--network=host` - Capability expansion: `--cap-add ALL`, `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` - Security overrides: `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`, `--security-opt apparmor=unconfined` - Device access: `--device`, `--device-cgroup-rule` - Volume inheritance: `--volumes-from` - Runtime controls: `--runtime`, `--cgroup-parent`

CVE-2026-73804.title: User-scoped tokens can mint unscoped HTTP signature API credentials
CVE-2026-73804.description: ### Summary Gitea allow a `write:user` token to create an SSH public key that then authenticates to the API through HTTP Signature without any API token scope. The vulnerable chain is: 1. A token with only `write:user` cannot directly call unrelated API categories such as `write:admin`. 2. The same token can call `POST /api/v1/user/keys` and add an attacker-controlled SSH public key to the token owner's account. 3. The matching private key can sign API requests through Gitea's HTTP Signature authentication. 4. `HTTPSign.Verify()` authenticates the request as the key owner and sets `IsApiToken=true`, but it does not set `ApiTokenScope`. 5. `tokenRequiresScopes()` skips route-level scope enforcement when `IsApiToken=true` but `ApiTokenScope` is absent. The result is a token-to-credential escalation. The attacker starts with a user-scoped token and ends with an unscoped API authentication method for the same account. The resulting access is still constrained by the account's normal Gitea RBAC, but it bypasses the API token scope boundary. ### Details The API auth group accepts HTTP Signature authentication for API routes: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:769-780 func buildAuthGroup() *auth.Group { group := auth.NewGroup( &auth.OAuth2{}, &auth.HTTPSign{}, &auth.Basic{}, // FIXME: this should be removed once we don't allow basic auth in API ) if setting.Service.EnableReverseProxyAuthAPI { group.Add(&auth.ReverseProxy{}) // TODO: does it still make sense to support reverse proxy auth in API? } // others: API doesn't support SSPI auth because the caller should use token return group } ``` When a request contains a valid HTTP Signature, Gitea resolves the SSH key owner and marks the request as API-token authenticated: ```go // services/auth/httpsign.go:39-86 // Verify extracts and validates HTTPsign from the Signature header of the request and returns // the corresponding user object on successful validation. // Returns nil if header is empty or validation fails. func (h *HTTPSign) Verify(req *http.Request, w http.ResponseWriter, store DataStore, sess SessionStore) (*user_model.User, error) { sigHead := req.Header.Get('Signature') if len(sigHead) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } var ( publicKey *asymkey_model.PublicKey err error ) if len(req.Header.Get('X-Ssh-Certificate')) != 0 { // Handle Signature signed by SSH certificates if len(setting.SSH.TrustedUserCAKeys) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } publicKey, err = VerifyCert(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyCert on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } else { // Handle Signature signed by Public Key publicKey, err = VerifyPubKey(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyPubKey on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } u, err := user_model.GetUserByID(req.Context(), publicKey.OwnerID) if err != nil { log.Error('GetUserByID: %v', err) return nil, err } store.GetData()['IsApiToken'] = true log.Trace('HTTP Sign: Logged in user %-v', u) return u, nil } ``` That path does not assign `ApiTokenScope`. The route-level scope middleware is fail-open for that state. It only checks required scopes when both `IsApiToken=true` and `ApiTokenScope` exists: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:319-363 func tokenRequiresScopes(requiredScopeCategories ...auth_model.AccessTokenScopeCategory) func(ctx *context.APIContext) { return func(ctx *context.APIContext) { // no scope required if len(requiredScopeCategories) == 0 { return } // Need OAuth2 token to be present. scope, scopeExists := ctx.Data['ApiTokenScope'].(auth_model.AccessTokenScope) if ctx.Data['IsApiToken'] != true || !scopeExists { return } // use the http method to determine the access level requiredScopeLevel := auth_model.Read if ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPost || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPut || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPatch || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodDelete { requiredScopeLevel = auth_model.Write } // get the required scope for the given access level and category requiredScopes := auth_model.GetRequiredScopes(requiredScopeLevel, requiredScopeCategories...) allow, err := scope.HasScope(requiredScopes...) if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'checking scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } if !allow { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, fmt.Sprintf('token does not have at least one of required scope(s), required=%v, token scope=%v', requiredScopes, scope)) return } ctx.Data['requiredScopeCategories'] = requiredScopeCategories // check if scope only applies to public resources publicOnly, err := scope.PublicOnly() if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'parsing public resource scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } // assign to true so that those searching should only filter public repositories/users/organizations ctx.PublicOnly = publicOnly } } ``` Therefore, a signed HTTP Signature request proceeds to the handler and normal account RBAC without checking `write:admin`, `write:repository`, `write:organization`, or other token categories. The key-enrollment route is available through the user scope group: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:1086-1091 m.Group('/keys', func() { m.Combo('').Get(user.ListMyPublicKeys). Post(bind(api.CreateKeyOption{}), user.CreatePublicKey) m.Combo('/{id}').Get(user.GetPublicKey). Delete(user.DeletePublicKey) }, rejectPublicOnly()) ``` `CreatePublicKey()` stores the supplied key for the authenticated user: ```go // routers/api/v1/user/key.go:202-249 func CreateUserPublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext, form api.CreateKeyOption, uid int64) { if user_model.IsFeatureDisabledWithLoginType(ctx.Doer, setting.UserFeatureManageSSHKeys) { ctx.APIErrorNotFound('Not Found', errors.New('ssh keys setting is not allowed to be visited')) return } content, err := asymkey_model.CheckPublicKeyString(form.Key) if err != nil { repo.HandleCheckKeyStringError(ctx, err) return } key, err := asymkey_model.AddPublicKey(ctx, uid, form.Title, content, 0, false) if err != nil { repo.HandleAddKeyError(ctx, err) return } apiLink := composePublicKeysAPILink() apiKey := convert.ToPublicKey(apiLink, key) if ctx.Doer.IsAdmin || ctx.Doer.ID == key.OwnerID { apiKey, _ = appendPrivateInformation(ctx, apiKey, key, ctx.Doer) } ctx.JSON(http.StatusCreated, apiKey) } // CreatePublicKey create one public key for me func CreatePublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext) { // swagger:operation POST /user/keys user userCurrentPostKey // --- // summary: Create a public key // consumes: // - application/json // produces: // - application/json // parameters: // - name: body // in: body // schema: // '$ref': '#/definitions/CreateKeyOption' // responses: // '201': // '$ref': '#/responses/PublicKey' // '422': // '$ref': '#/responses/validationError' form := web.GetForm(ctx).(*api.CreateKeyOption) CreateUserPublicKey(ctx, *form, ctx.Doer.ID) } ``` This means a `write:user` token can enroll an attacker-controlled key, and that key then becomes an unscoped HTTP Signature API credential. ### PoC ```http # Control: the original write:user token cannot directly use admin scope. POST /api/v1/admin/users Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'username':'scope-control','email':'scope-control@example.invalid','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'scope-control','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 403 Forbidden # Enroll an attacker-controlled SSH public key with the same write:user token. POST /api/v1/user/keys Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'title':'httpsig-api-key','key':'ssh-rsa {attacker-public-key}'} # Expected: 201 Created # Sign an admin API request with the matching private key. The Signature keyId is # the SSH fingerprint of the enrolled public key, and the signed headers include # (request-target), (created), and (expires). POST /api/v1/admin/users Signature: keyId='{ssh-key-fingerprint}',algorithm='{ssh-signature-algorithm}',headers='(request-target) (created) (expires)',signature='{base64-signature}' Content-Type: application/json {'username':'created-by-httpsig','email':'created-by-httpsig@example.com','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'created-by-httpsig','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 201 Created when the key owner is a site admin ``` ### Impact The attacker can enroll an SSH key and use HTTP Signature to reach any API category allowed by the victim account's normal RBAC. For a site-admin victim, the PoC shows access to `POST /api/v1/admin/users` without `write:admin`. For a non-admin victim, the same unscoped HTTP Signature credential can reach repository, package, organization, issue, or notification APIs according to the user's account permissions, without the corresponding token scopes. Destructive operations are also available where the victim account has the corresponding RBAC, such as repository/package deletion or admin-managed resource changes.
